records.place: Loreto Aprutino, province of Pescara, Trebbiano d'Abruzzo DOC, Abruzzo

wine.name: Trebbiano d'Abruzzo
wine.classification: DOC, Italy's controlled designation of origin, recognised for Trebbiano d'Abruzzo in 1972
wine.grapes: Trebbiano Abruzzese, the region's own Trebbiano, rather than the Trebbiano Toscano that the rule also allows.
wine.sites: The family's hillside vineyards around Loreto Aprutino, inland from Pescara and within reach of the Adriatic; only part of the crop is ever bottled under the family name.
wine.making: Aged in large old oak casks rather than small barrels, then released late, when the house judges it ready. Only the lots the family accepts are bottled, the rest of the crop is sold, and in some years no Trebbiano is released at all. The house says little of its methods.
wine.glass: Smoke, yellow apple and hay over salted lemon when young, turning waxy and nutty with age; full in texture yet dry and saline, with fresh, steady acidity and a long, savoury finish.
wine.ageing: It opens slowly over its first years in bottle and, from a sound cellar, can live for decades.
wine.serve: 10 to 13 degrees Celsius, cool rather than cold; open a young bottle an hour ahead or decant it; a large white wine glass.

label.means: The region's white DOC, recognised in 1972, from Trebbiano Abruzzese or Trebbiano Toscano.
Italy's controlled designation of origin, the tier below DOCG; Trebbiano d'Abruzzo has no DOCG.

records.table: Valentini's Trebbiano d'Abruzzo comes from the family's hillside vines at Loreto Aprutino, aged in large old casks and bottled only in the years the house accepts. Smoky, saline and slow to open, it shows how long a Trebbiano can live; pour it cool, not cold.
records.story: The Valentini family has held land at Loreto Aprutino, in the hills inland from Pescara, since the seventeenth century, by one account from 1650. Its modern story is that of Edoardo Valentini, who died in 2006. In the 1950s he gave up a career in the law to return to the family estate, and set out to prove that Trebbiano d'Abruzzo, a name known mostly for plain white wine, could give a white of depth that lasts for decades. He sold most of the crop, a habit the house has kept, and bottled only the lots he judged worthy, so that in some years no Trebbiano appeared at all. He worked in large old casks rather than small new barrels, spoke little of his methods, and the estate's reticence became part of its story. In 1972 Trebbiano d'Abruzzo became a DOC, a name that came to cover much plain white wine, and Valentini's bottle is the one teachers reach for to show what the same name can hold. After his death in 2006 his son took the estate on along the same lines. For a sommelier, Valentini's Trebbiano is the answer to anyone who judges a wine by its grape or its appellation: a humble name, and a white that lives for decades.

others.name: Montepulciano d'Abruzzo
others.note: The house's red, structured and long lived, and like the white not made in every vintage.

others.name: Cerasuolo d'Abruzzo
others.note: The house's rosato of Montepulciano, given the same patient treatment as the red and the white.

traps: Valentini of Loreto Aprutino is not La Valentina, a different Abruzzo estate that also bottles Trebbiano d'Abruzzo.
Trebbiano d'Abruzzo is a DOC, not a DOCG, and the vine behind Valentini's wine is Trebbiano Abruzzese, not Trebbiano Toscano.
A missing year in a run of Valentini is the house's choice, not a gap in the list: not every vintage is released.

cards.front: Valentini: which Trebbiano grows in the Loreto Aprutino vineyards for its Trebbiano d'Abruzzo?
cards.back: Trebbiano Abruzzese, the region's own vine, rather than the Trebbiano Toscano the DOC also allows.

cards.front: Who made Valentini's name, and in which decade did he return to the family estate?
cards.back: Edoardo Valentini, who gave up the law in the 1950s and died in 2006.

questions.q: A guest notices that a vintage of Valentini's Trebbiano d'Abruzzo is missing from the list. Which explanation fits the house?
opts: It bottles only the lots and years it accepts
Its DOC forbids any release in cool years
The wine is sold only after ten years
Its vines are replanted every few years
questions.exp: The house sells most of its crop and bottles only the lots it judges worthy, so some vintages never appear; no rule of the DOC forbids a release in a cool year.

questions.q: Before he turned his family's Loreto Aprutino estate towards bottled Trebbiano in the 1950s, which career did Edoardo Valentini give up?
opts: The law
Medicine
Banking
Architecture
questions.exp: He left a career in law to return to the family estate and made the house's name until his death in 2006; no account gives him a career in medicine.

report: Searches for this record: 7 of the group's share of 35; the group used 33, three of them shared on the appellations, and one fetch (emidiopepe.com) was refused. Valentini has no site the search reached, so the record rests on the library, two press accounts (WineNews, Decanter), two merchants' pages and the consorzio's disciplinare.

Edoardo Valentini's death in 2006 is in WineNews (30 April 2006) and Fine and Rare Wines (at 72), but no source read gives his birth year, 1933 or 1934 by that age, so he carries his death alone. Living names met, none in the fragment, for people.json: Francesco Paolo Valentini, his wife Elena Valentini and their son Gabriele Valentini.

The roots in Loreto Aprutino from 1650 are WineNews's, and Fine and Rare Wines says since the 1600s, hence the seventeenth century; the first commercial vintage of 1956 is Fine and Rare Wines' alone and is left as the 1950s. The law career rests on Fine and Rare Wines and IT Wine Club.

The plan's why (old pergola vines) and the region record (the two estates that keep their tendone) speak of pergola, but two searches found no source that says so of Valentini's own vineyards, so training is left out; Decanter speaks of tendone in Abruzzo at large.

vino.com's sheets for 2018 and 2020 give fermentation with native yeasts in large casks, about a year in casks of 50 and 70 hectolitres and bottling without filtration, and Scatti di Gusto says no barrique, only large casks; one merchant's two pages are not two sources, so the making keeps the library's large old wood and late release, and the refuter may settle the rest.
The soil (sandy, calcareous clay) is Fine and Rare Wines' alone and is left out; the share of vintages released (about seven in ten) is one merchant's and is left out.
La Valentina, the trap's other estate, is a different producer whose Trebbiano d'Abruzzo is listed by two merchants (Dalla Terra, Superiore.de); no library record is in tension with this one.

records.place: Torano Nuovo, province of Teramo, Montepulciano d'Abruzzo DOC, Abruzzo

wine.name: Montepulciano d'Abruzzo
wine.classification: DOC, Italy's controlled designation of origin, the tier below DOCG
wine.grapes: Montepulciano alone, from the family's own vineyards around Torano Nuovo.
wine.sites: The family's vineyards on the hills of Torano Nuovo in the north of Abruzzo, where the house began on a small plot in 1964; many vines are trained on the traditional pergola and farmed organically and biodynamically.
wine.making: The Montepulciano is destemmed by hand, rubbed over a net on a wooden vat so the berries fall through and the stems stay behind, then fermented in glass lined cement tanks, some in use since 1964. It ages in cement, with no wood at all, is bottled unfiltered and then rests in the house's cellar, often for many years before release.
wine.glass: Sour cherry, black cherry and dried plum with blood orange peel, wild herbs and a smoky, tarry note; medium to full in body, with lively acidity, grippy tannin that turns silky with age, and no taste of oak.
wine.ageing: Fierce when young and built for the long haul: the house keeps a deep library of old vintages and releases some of them decades after the harvest.
wine.serve: 16 to 18 degrees Celsius; decant a young bottle an hour ahead and an old one gently off its sediment; a large Burgundy glass.

label.means: The region's red DOC; Montepulciano is the grape here, not the Tuscan town.
Italy's controlled designation of origin, the tier the house's red carries.

records.table: Emidio Pepe's Montepulciano d'Abruzzo comes from Torano Nuovo: hand destemmed grapes, fermented and aged in glass lined cement with no wood, bottled unfiltered. Sour cherry, blood orange and wild herbs; old vintages are decanted at the house before release and want a gentle decanting again.
records.story: The Pepe family made wine at Torano Nuovo, in the hills of Teramo, from 1899 by its own account, but sold it in bulk. Emidio Pepe (1932 to 2026), born into that farming family, began bottling under his own name in 1964, starting with a small plot near the village and the glass lined cement tanks the cellar has used ever since. From the start he held that Montepulciano d'Abruzzo could make one of the great reds of Italy, and he made it by hand: the red grapes destemmed over a net, the white Trebbiano trodden by foot in wooden tubs, no oak at all. Rather than sell every vintage young, the family kept back part of each harvest in its cellar, and before an old vintage leaves the house each bottle is opened, decanted off its sediment, topped up from a second bottle of the same year and corked again, the year of decanting printed on the cork. His daughters and then a granddaughter worked beside him, and he died at Torano Nuovo on 28 July 2026, a day after his ninety fourth birthday. For a sommelier, Pepe stands for Montepulciano made slowly: no wood, years in the cellar, released when the house judges it ready.

others.name: Trebbiano d'Abruzzo
others.note: The house's white, its grapes trodden by foot in wooden tubs; with Valentini's, the long lived Trebbiano a candidate is expected to know.

others.name: Pecorino
others.note: A revived white grape of Abruzzo bottled on its own; the name has nothing to do with the cheese.

traps: Pepe's Montepulciano sees no oak: fermentation and ageing are in glass lined cement, so a toasty, vanilla note in a blind wine argues against it.
Only the white Trebbiano is trodden by foot; the Montepulciano is destemmed by hand over a net.
Montepulciano d'Abruzzo is the grape of Abruzzo, never Vino Nobile di Montepulciano, the Sangiovese of the Tuscan town.

cards.front: Emidio Pepe: in what vessels is the Montepulciano fermented and aged?
cards.back: Glass lined cement tanks, some in use since 1964, with no wood at all.

cards.front: What does the house do to an old vintage of Emidio Pepe before it is released?
cards.back: Each bottle is decanted off its sediment, topped up from a bottle of the same year and corked again, the year of decanting printed on the cork.

questions.q: At a tasting of Emidio Pepe, a guest asks how the Montepulciano grapes are handled before fermentation. Which answer fits the house?
opts: Destemmed by hand over a net on a wooden vat
Trodden by foot with their stems in wooden tubs
Crushed by machine and chilled for a week
Fermented as whole bunches in small oak barrels
questions.exp: The house destems the Montepulciano by hand over a net so the berries fall through; treading by foot in wooden tubs is kept for the white Trebbiano.

questions.q: In which year did Emidio Pepe first put the family's wine into a bottle under his own name?
questions.exp: The first bottle with the Emidio Pepe label was of 1964; 1899 is when the family began making wine, by its account, and 1932 the year of his birth.

report: Searches for this record: 5 of the group's share, and the one fetch of the group, the house's method page, was refused (emidiopepe.com does not resolve here); the house's own pages were read through search.

The plan's note is answered: Emidio Pepe died at home at Torano Nuovo on 28 July 2026, aged 94, a day after his birthday (Sky TG24, Gambero Rosso, Wine Spectator, Wein.plus), and the Noble Rot profile gives his birth in 1932, so he is named with his dates.

Living names met, none in the fragment, for people.json: his daughters Sofia Pepe and Daniela Pepe, his granddaughters Chiara De Iulis Pepe and Elisa De Iulis Pepe; his wife, named by one merchant, is not named for want of her status.

Library tension: p-emidio-pepe's style says the grapes are crushed by foot, and the region record says one Teramo estate crushes by foot; the house's own method page says the Montepulciano is destemmed by hand over a net and only the Trebbiano is trodden by foot in a wooden tub, which the record follows.
The library's founded 1964 is kept: the house dates the family's winemaking to 1899, by the founder's grandfather of the same name, and its first labelled bottle to 1964.

The time in cement (24 months by Vinous, two years by a merchant) is left as ages in cement, and the fermentation's length (eight days, ten to twelve, twenty eight to thirty) disagrees and is left out; bottled unfiltered rests on a merchant's page, the region record and the plan, and the refuter should confirm it against the house.

Left out for one source or disagreement: the parcels Casa Pepe (planted 1974) and Branella (1966), the Montepulciano selection the house traces to 1890, and the age past which old bottles are decanted (over ten years by one account, over twenty by another).

records.place: San Martino sulla Marrucina, province of Chieti, Abruzzo

wine.name: Villa Gemma Montepulciano d'Abruzzo Riserva
wine.classification: Riserva, the longer aged type of the Montepulciano d'Abruzzo DOC
wine.grapes: Montepulciano alone, by the house's sheets.
wine.sites: Colle Cave at San Martino sulla Marrucina, about 400 metres up in the hills of Chieti, on clay with limestone and facing south east; the vines are trained on Guyot in close rows rather than on the old pergola.
wine.making: By the house's sheets it ferments in stainless steel with twenty to thirty days on its skins, then ages in new or first fill French oak barriques, for twelve to eighteen months by vintage, and rests at least two years in bottle before release.
wine.glass: Black plum and liquorice over mocha and vanilla from the new oak; full bodied and dense, with ripe, soft tannin, moderate acidity and a warm finish.
wine.ageing: Released ready to drink after its years at the house, it holds and gains savoury notes for many years in a cool cellar.
wine.serve: 16 to 18 degrees Celsius; decant a young bottle an hour ahead; a large Bordeaux glass.

label.means: The house's name for its leading line of wines, first given to the red of 1984.
The DOC's longer aged type; Villa Gemma rests for years in barrel and bottle before release.
The region's red DOC, from the Montepulciano grape, not the Tuscan town.

records.table: Masciarelli's Villa Gemma Riserva is Montepulciano d'Abruzzo from one hillside at San Martino sulla Marrucina, aged in French barriques and then for years in bottle. Dense and polished, with black plum, liquorice and mocha, it is the modern face of the grape; decant it for roast meat.
records.story: Gianni Masciarelli, who died in 2008, learnt his love of the vine from his maternal grandfather, by the house's account, and in 1981 founded his own estate at San Martino sulla Marrucina in the hills of Chieti; its first vintage gave some 700 bottles of Montepulciano d'Abruzzo and 1,300 of Trebbiano d'Abruzzo. At a time when most of Abruzzo's wine left the region in bulk, he set out to give the native grapes a polish that would carry them abroad: close planted vines on Guyot beside the old pergola, and French barriques for the leading wines. With the 1984 vintage he made the first Villa Gemma, a Montepulciano from San Martino, and it became the wine through which the house found its style. In 1987 he met the partner of his life and work, and by the house's account their partnership gave the estate its reach abroad. On 31 July 2008 he died suddenly on a business trip to Munich, and his partner and his daughter took the estate on. For a sommelier, Villa Gemma is the other pole of Abruzzo from Valentini and Pepe: Montepulciano ripened, oaked and polished for the tables of the world.

others.name: La Botte di Gianni
others.note: A Montepulciano d'Abruzzo Riserva of the house, named for its founder.

others.name: Villa Gemma Cerasuolo
others.note: The line's rosato of Montepulciano, from vines kept on the traditional Abruzzo pergola.

others.name: Villa Gemma Bianco
others.note: The line's white, sold as Abruzzo Bianco DOC, also from pergola trained vines.

traps: Villa Gemma comes in three colours, a red Riserva, a Cerasuolo and a white; the flagship is the red Montepulciano d'Abruzzo Riserva.
Masciarelli is the modern pole of Abruzzo, French barriques and ripe fruit, the opposite of Pepe's cement and Valentini's large old casks.

cards.front: Masciarelli's Villa Gemma Riserva: which vineyard gives it, and how are its vines trained?
cards.back: Colle Cave at San Martino sulla Marrucina, about 400 metres up, on Guyot in close rows rather than pergola.

cards.front: By Masciarelli's own account, who gave its founder his love of the vine?
cards.back: His maternal grandfather; the founder started his own estate at San Martino sulla Marrucina in 1981.

questions.q: A guest compares Masciarelli's Villa Gemma Riserva with Emidio Pepe's Montepulciano and asks where its vanilla and mocha come from. Which answer fits?
opts: Ageing in French oak barriques
Fermentation in glass lined cement
Years in large old Slavonian casks
Grapes dried on mats before pressing
questions.exp: Villa Gemma ages twelve to eighteen months in new or first fill French barriques; Pepe's red sees only cement, and large old casks give little vanilla.

questions.q: Masciarelli was founded in 1981. What did its founder first bottle under the Villa Gemma name, with the 1984 vintage?
opts: A Montepulciano red from San Martino
A barrel fermented Trebbiano
A Cerasuolo d'Abruzzo rosato
A sparkling Pecorino
questions.exp: By the house's sheets the first Villa Gemma, of 1984, was a Montepulciano from San Martino sulla Marrucina; the line's white and rosato are not the wine first made under the name.

Masciarelli Store: Villa Gemma Montepulciano d'Abruzzo DOC Riserva 2018
Masciarelli: press kit

report: Searches for this record: 5 of the group's share.

The plan's note is answered in part: Gianni Masciarelli died on 31 July 2008 in Munich (Decanter, WineNews), but Decanter gives his age as 53 and a forum and a travel site 52, so his birth year is uncertain and he carries his death alone.

Living names met, none in the fragment, for people.json: Marina Cvetic, his partner, and Miriam Lee Masciarelli, his daughter, who led the house from 2008 by its own account; the library's holdings line and two of its wines (Marina Cvetic Montepulciano d'Abruzzo Riserva and Trebbiano d'Abruzzo Marina Cvetic) carry her name, so this record leaves those wines out of others and the library may wish to look again.
Library tension: p-masciarelli's first trap names Abruzzo's DOCGs as Colline Teramane and Tullum, while the region record adds Casauria, recognised in 2025, so the trap may be out of date.

The label: the house's sheets print Villa Gemma Montepulciano d'Abruzzo DOC Riserva (the 2018 vintage); the region record says that from the 2023 harvest Riserva is reserved for wines of the sub-zones, so later vintages may add a sub-zone name, which this record does not print.

The barrique time differs by sheet, twelve months in first passage barriques on the English sheet and eighteen in new ones on the Italian sheet of 2018, hence twelve to eighteen months by vintage; the first vintage of 1984 is on the house's sheets and in Decanter.

Left out: the Gambero Rosso guide's naming of the 1995 as the wine of the year of Italy in 2000 (an award and a ranking), the meaning of the name Villa Gemma (not found), the year the house took on the Castello di Semivicoli (not found), and a start at his father's winery in 1978 (one source).

records.place: Controguerra, province of Teramo, Colline Teramane DOCG, Abruzzo

wine.name: Zanna Montepulciano d'Abruzzo Colline Teramane Riserva
wine.classification: DOCG, Italy's guaranteed tier, granted to Colline Teramane by decree of 20 February 2003
wine.grapes: Montepulciano alone, from the estate's Zanna vineyard.
wine.sites: The Zanna vineyard at Controguerra, the estate's first historic plot, at about 280 metres on close, marly soil with clay; its name, the house says, recalls the wolves that once roamed there.
wine.making: Destemmed and crushed, the grapes ferment in stainless steel at no more than 30 degrees Celsius. After the malolactic the wine moves to casks of Slavonian oak of about 25 hectolitres for 24 to 26 months, then rests at least two years in bottle before release; it is made only in the vintages the house judges right.
wine.glass: Plum, blackberry and liquorice over tar and a dusty note of the cask; full bodied, with firm, ripe tannin and a long, dark finish.
wine.ageing: Firm and dark on release, after years at the house, it opens over several more in bottle and keeps for many after that.
wine.serve: 16 to 18 degrees Celsius; decant a young bottle an hour or two ahead; a large Bordeaux glass.

label.means: The DOCG of the hills of Teramo province, granted in 2003, for Montepulciano.
Under the DOCG, at least three years of ageing before the wine is released.
The vineyard at Controguerra the family bought in 1960, named, the house says, for wolves.

records.table: Illuminati's Zanna is a Montepulciano d'Abruzzo Colline Teramane Riserva from the vineyard the family bought at Controguerra in 1960, aged two years in large Slavonian oak casks and two more in bottle. Plum, blackberry, liquorice and tar over firm tannin; decant it for roast lamb.
records.story: The house dates itself to 1890, when its founder opened a winery he called Fattoria Nicò at Ripatransone, in the Marche just across the border from Abruzzo. In 1960 his grandson, Dino Illuminati, crossed to the Abruzzo side of the hills, to Controguerra in the province of Teramo, and bought a farmhouse and its land in a place called Zanna, a name the house links to the wolves that once roamed there. He was among the early growers of the area to bottle Montepulciano d'Abruzzo rather than sell it in bulk, and he worked for the appellations of his hills: the Controguerra DOC and then the Montepulciano d'Abruzzo Colline Teramane DOCG, granted by decree of 20 February 2003, the DOCG of the Teramo hills. The Zanna vineyard, his first plot there, gives the house's long aged Riserva, made only in the vintages it judges right. Dino Illuminati died at home in February 2023, at 92, and the family carried the estate on, five generations from the founder by the house's count. For a sommelier, Zanna is a Colline Teramane to know: Montepulciano of the northern hills, aged in large casks and built to keep.

others.name: Pieluni
others.note: A second Montepulciano d'Abruzzo Colline Teramane Riserva of the house.

traps: Zanna is a vineyard and a wine, not a sub-zone: the appellation on the label is Montepulciano d'Abruzzo Colline Teramane DOCG.
Illuminati began in the Marche, at Ripatransone in 1890; it has been at Controguerra, in Abruzzo, since 1960.
Colline Teramane is the DOCG of the Teramo hills; a plain Montepulciano d'Abruzzo from the same hills is a DOC wine.

cards.front: Illuminati's Zanna: what is it aged in after the malolactic, and for how long?
cards.back: Casks of Slavonian oak of about 25 hectolitres, for 24 to 26 months, then at least two years in bottle.

cards.front: Where did Illuminati begin in 1890, and when did it move to Controguerra?
cards.back: At Ripatransone in the Marche, as Fattoria Nicò; the founder's grandson moved to Controguerra in 1960.

questions.q: A guest asks which appellation Illuminati's Zanna carries on its label. Which is it?
opts: Montepulciano d'Abruzzo Colline Teramane DOCG
Montepulciano d'Abruzzo Terre di Chieti DOC
Vino Nobile di Montepulciano DOCG
Controguerra Rosso DOC
questions.exp: Zanna is a Riserva of the Colline Teramane DOCG, granted in 2003; Controguerra is a separate DOC of the same commune, not the label Zanna carries.

questions.q: In 1960 the founder's grandson moved Illuminati from the Marche to Controguerra and bought land at Zanna. What, by the house's account, does the name Zanna recall?
opts: The wolves that once roamed there
A saint of the parish church
A family of local landowners
A fang shaped bend of a river
questions.exp: The house says the name recalls the wolves that once roamed those lands; zanna is Italian for a fang, but no river bend is meant.

report: Searches for this record: 8 of the group's share, one of them empty on illuminativini.it before the house's domain was found to be illuminativini.com.

The house began at Ripatransone in the Marche in 1890 as Fattoria Nicò and has been at Controguerra since 1960, by its own history page; the plan's why and the region record's producers line call it a Controguerra house of 1890, true of the house but not of the place.

The founder is described rather than named: no source gives his dates, and the house says a living descendant of five generations on bears the same name. Living names met, none in the fragment, for people.json: Nicola Illuminati (the living one), Stefano Illuminati and Lorenzo Illuminati.

Dino Illuminati died at home at 92 (Gambero Rosso's obituary of 15 February 2023; Doctor Wine), and his birth year, 1930 or 1931, is in neither, so he carries his death alone; Gambero Rosso says he took the estate on in the 1950s and the house says he moved to Controguerra in 1960, so the record keeps 1960.

The plan calls the house a founder of the Colline Teramane DOCG; Gambero Rosso calls Dino Illuminati an early champion of the Controguerra DOC and the Colline Teramane DOCG, and a guide (Vinoscout) says he fought for the Controguerra DOC of 1996, so the story says he worked for both and gives no year for the DOC.
Left out: Zanna's first vintage (not found), tendone training at about 1,100 vines a hectare (one sales sheet), and the house's vineyard size (volatile and in conflict, 110 or 130 hectares).

The marl and clay, the steel at no more than 30 degrees, the casks of about 25 hectolitres for 24 to 26 months and the two years in bottle are on the house's Zanna page; Slavonian oak and the vintages only it judges right are on its English page and two merchants' (Superiore.de, Bottle of Italy).

records.place: Ofena, province of L'Aquila, Cerasuolo d'Abruzzo DOC, Abruzzo

wine.name: Piè delle Vigne Cerasuolo d'Abruzzo
wine.classification: DOC, Cerasuolo d'Abruzzo's own since 2010, before that a type of Montepulciano d'Abruzzo
wine.grapes: Montepulciano alone, from the house's vineyards at Ofena.
wine.sites: The house's vineyards around Ofena, between about 320 and 440 metres, in a small plateau shaped like an amphitheatre under the Gran Sasso that locals call the Forno d'Abruzzo, the oven of Abruzzo.
wine.making: By the house's account it is made by svacata, an old step of the farmhouse cellars: part of the Montepulciano ferments as a white wine, off its skins, and part as a red, and about halfway through the fermentation the red is drawn off its skins and joined to the white. It then spends a year in stainless steel and a year in bottle.
wine.glass: Deep cherry red; wild raspberry, sour cherry and red cherry with almond and a stony note; dry and vinous, with fresh acidity, a light grip of tannin and a bitter almond finish.
wine.ageing: Ready when it is released, after its year in bottle, it keeps its fruit and gains depth for a few years more.
wine.serve: 10 to 12 degrees Celsius, cooler than a red and warmer than a pale rosé; no need to decant; a white wine glass.

label.means: Abruzzo's DOC for rosato of Montepulciano, named for its cherry colour; its own DOC since 2010.
The house's name for this Cerasuolo, Italian for the foot of the vines, first made in 1997.

records.table: Cataldi Madonna's Piè delle Vigne is a Cerasuolo d'Abruzzo of Montepulciano from Ofena, under the Gran Sasso, made by the old svacata method, part of a red fermentation joined to a white. Deep cherry red, with wild raspberry and almond; pour it cool.
records.story: By the house's own account its work with the vine at Ofena began in 1920 under a baron of the family, and it was his son who first bottled wine under the family name, in 1975. Since that year the labels have carried the Warrior of Capestrano, the ancient stone statue found near the vineyards. In 1988 the bottler's son made the Montepulciano Tonì in his father's honour, and in 1990 he took the estate on. Ofena lies in the small basin that locals call the oven of Abruzzo, under the Gran Sasso. With the 1997 vintage it first made Piè delle Vigne by svacata, an old step of the farmhouse cellars in which part of the must is drawn off a red fermentation halfway through and joined to a white one. Cerasuolo d'Abruzzo, from 1968 a type of the Montepulciano d'Abruzzo DOC, became a DOC of its own in 2010, and the house's grapes have been certified organic since 2016, by its account. For a sommelier, Piè delle Vigne is the answer to a guest who thinks rosé a light summer wine: Cerasuolo is cherry coloured and vinous, made for food.

others.name: Tonì
others.note: The house's Montepulciano d'Abruzzo, first made in 1988 and named for its maker's father; aged in a 25 hectolitre cask since 2017, in barriques before.

others.name: Giulia
others.note: The house's Pecorino, sold as IGT Terre d'Abruzzo; Supergiulia is its double selection of vineyards and grapes.

traps: Cerasuolo d'Abruzzo is a rosato of Montepulciano; Cerasuolo di Vittoria is a Sicilian red DOCG.
Cerasuolo d'Abruzzo has been a DOC of its own since 2010; before that it was a type of the Montepulciano d'Abruzzo DOC.
Svacata joins part of a red fermentation, drawn off halfway, to a white one; it is not a blend of finished red and white wine.

cards.front: Cataldi Madonna's Piè delle Vigne: what is the svacata method behind it?
cards.back: Part of the must is drawn off a red fermentation about halfway through and joined to a white fermentation of the same grape.

cards.front: In what basin under the Gran Sasso does Cataldi Madonna grow its Montepulciano?
cards.back: Around Ofena, in the small amphitheatre that locals call the Forno d'Abruzzo, the oven of Abruzzo.

questions.q: A guest is surprised by the deep cherry colour of Cataldi Madonna's Piè delle Vigne. Which grape and appellation explain it?
opts: Montepulciano, as Cerasuolo d'Abruzzo DOC
Sangiovese, as Toscana Rosato IGT
Nero d'Avola, as Cerasuolo di Vittoria DOCG
Aglianico, as Campania Rosato IGT
questions.exp: Cerasuolo d'Abruzzo is a rosato of Montepulciano, a grape deep in colour; Cerasuolo di Vittoria shares the word but is a Sicilian red DOCG, not a rosato.

questions.q: With which vintage did Cataldi Madonna first make its Piè delle Vigne by the svacata method?
questions.exp: The house dates the first Piè delle Vigne to 1997; 1975 was its first bottling under the family name, 1990 the year the next generation took over and 2010 Cerasuolo's own DOC.

report: Searches for this record: 5 of the group's share; the house's pages were read through search.

The pick: no page of the house names one wine its flagship; Gambero Rosso's guide Vini d'Italia 2021 made the Piè delle Vigne 2018 its rosato of the year (an award, not used in prose), so the pick is kept as the group's rosato, with Tonì and the Pecorino Giulia under others.

The label: the house's shop and Falstaff print the 2024 vintage as Cerasuolo d'Abruzzo Superiore Terre Aquilane DOC, while older vintages read Cerasuolo d'Abruzzo DOC, so the record prints Cerasuolo d'Abruzzo alone; the region record names the L'Aquila sub-zone Terre de L'Aquila, where the ministry's single document and the label read Terre Aquilane.

Living names met, none in the fragment, for people.json: Luigi Cataldi Madonna (the son who made Tonì in 1988 and took over in 1990) and Giulia Cataldi Madonna; the baron of 1920, also Luigi Cataldi Madonna, and his son Antonio, who first bottled in 1975, are described, for no source gives their dates.

The relationship: the house's Tonì page says it was made in 1988 in honour of the maker's father Tonino, and its history says Antonio first bottled in 1975, so the record calls the man of 1988 the bottler's son; one search summary called him Antonio's nephew, a reading of the Italian nipote, and the refuter may wish to confirm.

The svacata is the house's account, with Gazzetta del Gusto's interview (part of the must drawn off about halfway through fermentation, first tried in 1997) as the second; a merchant's account of two pickings, about 85 and 15 per cent, and a maceration of four to five days are left out.

Region record tension: its producers line calls the estate the reference estate of Ofena on the high L'Aquila plateau, a word of judgement; the house puts its vines at 320 to 440 metres in a basin, which the record follows. The house's claim that the Calderone above it is the only glacier of the Apennines is left out.
Cerasuolo as a type of Montepulciano d'Abruzzo from 1968 is in the consorzio's disciplinare, and its own DOC by decree of 5 October 2010 in the European Union's eAmbrosia file.
